core_principles.text: Customize the squatting foot position, setup, and depth based on an individual's unique hip anthropometrics rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach.
Individuals with a retroverted femur typically require a more toed-out squat stance and need to rotate their hips outward when squatting.
Individuals with an anteverted femur typically tolerate a more toed-forward squat stance.

common_mistakes.text: Using a one-size-fits-all dogmatic approach to squatting instead of customizing the stance and setup to the individual's unique hip anatomy.

specific_findings.text: Normal femoral version features a femoral head and neck oriented forward at approximately 15 degrees.
The McKibbin Instability Index, which sums the versions of the femoral neck and hip socket, may be predictive of hip issues during squatting.

consequences.text: Ignoring individual variations in femoral and acetabular version when determining squat stance can lead to hip issues and compromise the longevity of the athlete.

source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 1/4]

core_principles.text: Perform an assessment of hip morphology to determine the proper customized squat stance for an individual's unique body.
Use the hip quadrant test in a supine position to assess the femoral acetabular joint's shape, size, and movement capacity without soft tissue restrictions.
Ensure the spine and pelvis remain in a neutral, fully supported position during the hip quadrant test, allowing only the tested lower extremity to move.
Test degrees of hip flexion, external rotation, and abduction synergistically to find the maximum pain-free hip flexion angle, which represents the anatomical limit for squat depth.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing compensation patterns in the pelvis, spine, or opposite extremity during hip mobility testing.
Ignoring individual anatomical variations in femoral version and acetabular orientation when prescribing squat stance and depth.

specific_findings.text: In one study, the average Caucasian male had 7 degrees of femoral anteversion (range -2 to 35 degrees) and the average Chinese male had 14 degrees of anteversion (range -4 to 36 degrees).
A study on femoral version showed retroversion rates of 24.1% in Caucasian males, 15.1% in African American males, and 14.3% in females of all ethnicities.

consequences.text: Exceeding the hip joint's anatomical limit (the theoretical glass ceiling on squat depth) forces compensation patterns, such as posterior pelvic tilt and spinal rounding.

source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 2/4]

core_principles.text: Centration of the hip joint maximizes the surface area contact of the femoral head into the acetabulum, which increases the activation of intrinsic stabilizers and optimizes the length-tension relationship of the gluteal and adductor groups.
Squat stance width and toe-out angle should be customized based on the individual's hip anatomy to maximize comfort, depth, and proper execution.
If maximal hip flexion is achieved with relatively more hip abduction during assessment, a wider squat stance may be more ideal for the athlete.
If ankle mobility is limited, a wider stance may be necessary to prevent the center of mass from being too far behind the base of support.
The degree of toe-out or external rotation at the hip joint should be adjusted to match the angle where maximal comfortable hip flexion is achieved.

common_mistakes.text: Squatting with a stance width or foot abduction angle that does not match the individual's anatomical capacity can lead to premature lumbar flexion.
Failing to widen the stance when ankle mobility is limited can cause the center of mass to fall too far behind the base of support.

specific_findings.text: The bilateral quadrant test uses four specific measurements to customize squat stance: buttocks-to-floor distance, distance between knee caps from the mid-patellar line, foot abduction angle from the foot's midline, and distance between heels at the mid-calcaneal line.

consequences.text: Forcing deep hip flexion without accommodating the necessary hip abduction and external rotation causes the pelvis to tilt posteriorly and the lumbar spine to flex.
Failing to adjust stance width when ankle mobility is limited shifts the center of mass too far behind the base of support, compromising balance.

source: data\squat\ANTHROPOMETRICAL CONSIDERATIONS FOR CUSTOMIZING THE SQUAT PATTERN.pdf [part 3/4]

core_principles.text: Athletes with more retroverted hips generally require a greater toe-out angle, or increased foot abduction, to achieve maximal hip flexion during a squat.
Athletes with more anteverted hips generally benefit from a relatively more toed-forward stance, or less foot abduction, during a squat.
To find the optimal squat stance, test a combination of stance widths with varying angles of toe-out, starting with the stance determined by a quadrant test.
Adjust stance width and toe-out angles to find the combination that allows the athlete to achieve the best squatting depth with the least compensations.
Athlete comfort should dictate the combination of stance width and toe-out, provided that biomechanical faults like knees collapsing in, lumbar flexion, or heels elevating are avoided.

common_mistakes.text: Allowing the knees to collapse inward during a squat is a biomechanical fault that must be avoided.
Allowing lumbar flexion during a squat is a biomechanical fault that must be avoided.
Allowing the heels to elevate during a squat is a biomechanical fault that must be avoided.
